doc.title: Bill Mays interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 5, 2025

title: Trio dynamics and An Ellington Affair with Nash and Goldsby
summary: The bass or drummer may drive the trio; he recalls the magical rehearsal-free Ellington Affair date.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: In a trio situation with bass and drums, like who’s driving the bus between those two people?

Well it varies on the twosome. Yeah. Who’s driving the bus. Sometimes it’s the bass player, sometimes it’s the drummer. Sometimes the drummer is playing a little on top of the beat a little too far and the bass player will hold it back, or vice versa. Sometimes it’s just perfect. And most of the time it’s just perfect ‘cause I call the right guys.
Yeah. There’s a learning curve to that and I’m sure that you mastered that a long time ago.

I remember, I did an album called “An Ellington Affair” for Concord records, all Duke and Billy Strayhorn tunes. And I’d never played with Lewis Nash and John Goldsby in a trio setting. I’d played with them in other groups. And I put them together for the date. We didn’t have a rehearsal, we just came into the studio, and man the recording is beautiful. And – ‘cause it was the right guys. They just locked it in from the minute we hit. And it was magic. So you know and I think it was magic because both those guys had had a ton of experience with different bands and different styles and so, you know it came together beautifully.
As you had all that experience.
